source.title: The Anisotropic Noise in Stochastic Gradient Descent: Its Behavior of Escaping from Sharp Minima and Regularization Effects
source.authors: Zhan-Xing Zhu; Jingfeng Wu; Bin Yu; Lei Wu; Jin-Wen Ma

record.file_problem: Full paper text is supplied, including supplementary material; no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: Compares SGD’s anisotropic noise with full-gradient methods using isotropic and other noise structures, and measures test accuracy and sharpness rather than directly testing the listed recipe factors or gap measures.
record.gate_note: Rows cover reported results comparing optimization dynamics and measuring their generalization-related outcomes. Cited results about large-batch training and flat minima are not included as rows. Figure-only curves without exact textual values are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study tests how gradient-noise covariance affects escape from minima and test accuracy, which no listed version claims. Its sharpness measure uses fixed isotropic perturbations rather than magnitude-scaled perturbations; it does not compare generalization-gap rankings. GD versus SGD at matched iterations also does not establish V5's fixed-epoch batch-size effect.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors argue that SGD's curvature-aligned anisotropic noise helps it escape sharp minima and reach flatter solutions with better generalization, whereas tuned isotropic noise does not reproduce these benefits in their experiments. Their theoretical escape analysis does not establish a general theorem connecting flatness to held-out performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares minibatch SGD with full-gradient descent plus several isotropic and anisotropic noise processes, rather than testing the claim versions' specified interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Generalization differs across noise structures and datasets; in FashionMNIST the four methods with curvature-aligned anisotropic noise escaped the GD solution while isotropic GLD variants and GD remained trapped. The paper states that effects of covariance structure are less obvious when learning rate is too small or batch size is overly large.

fits_no_version.finding: On partly corrupted FashionMNIST, SGD and curvature-aligned noise variants escape the GD solution and reach 68.74–68.90% test accuracy, versus 66.22–66.41% for GD and the other noise variants.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Curvature-aligned gradient noise can improve escape from a fitted minimum and subsequent test accuracy compared with isotropic or diagonal noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 1 reports SGD test accuracy of 75.21% on SVHN and 86.33% on CIFAR-10, exceeding GD and all tested GLD variants. Figure 6 separately reports improvements after initialization at GD solutions, subject to its inconsistent dataset attribution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noise covariance structure, beyond its overall magnitude, affects generalization in the tested VGG11 training settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Figures 3 and 6 associate successful escape and improved test accuracy with reduced expected loss increase under fixed isotropic weight perturbations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unscaled isotropic expected sharpness can accompany test-accuracy differences across noise-driven optimization trajectories.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 97, 2019
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the final test-accuracy comparisons. Main image-dataset comparisons use one model family without batch normalization and no data augmentation; FashionMNIST uses a small corrupted-label training set. Several exact results are available only in figure legends or curves.
record.rows_left_out: The toy example reports success rates and trajectories only graphically, without exact textual numerical results; Figure 2. The one-hidden-layer experiments report Tr(HΣ) and Tr(HΣ̄) graphically without exact text values; Figure 4. Sharpness curves and training-accuracy curves are also shown without exact values; Figures 3 and 6. These do not directly measure a version listed in the claim.

untested.parts: No paired natural-label and fully random-label training experiment with held-out performance is reported. Fitting a partly corrupted training set does not establish this comparison.
The width sweep measures noise-curvature alignment, not held-out error beyond the width needed to interpolate.
No convolutional versus fully connected generalization comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD held-out-performance comparison. Adam is used only to train networks for an alignment experiment.
No batch-size sweep under matched epoch budgets or evaluation of recipe adaptations. Equal GD and SGD iteration counts imply different data-processing budgets.
No dropout intervention; omitting dropout in VGG11 supplies no comparative evidence.
No magnitude-scaled perturbation measure, generalization-gap ranking, or comparison with norm- and margin-based measures. Fixed isotropic expected sharpness is a different measure.
No estimation of example memorization followed by selective removal and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: No listed version receives a verdict. All row states remain cannot_determine relative to those versions, even where the reported accuracy is readable. Figure 6 top-middle values were substantially mistranscribed. Its dataset caption also appears inconsistent with Figure 1's accuracy patterns; the supplied text does not resolve which dataset attribution is correct.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization versus natural-label generalization is not tested.
No width sweep across the interpolation threshold with natural-label test error is reported.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison is reported.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison is reported.
No large-batch versus small-batch comparison under fixed epoch budgets is reported.
The study measures expected sharpness under isotropic weight perturbations, not magnitude-aware sharpness or its ranking against other gap measures.
No memorized-example removal and retraining experiment is reported.
